name: Eating testicles / Rocky Mountain oysters
lead: Eating testicles, often as Rocky Mountain oysters, is the practice of consuming animal testicles in the belief that they support male hormones or virility. Rocky Mountain oysters are a dish of bulls' testicles, usually skinned and deep-fried [1].

The dish is traditionally associated with ranching and cattle castration, and many people consider it an aphrodisiac [1]. No clinical studies were found testing whether eating testicles changes human testosterone.
infobox: Prairie oysters, calf fries, criadillas, huevos de toro

paras: Rocky Mountain oysters are bull testicles that are skinned, coated in seasoned flour and deep-fried, and are sometimes pounded flat first [1]. Regional names include prairie oysters in Canada, calf fries in Oklahoma and the Texas Panhandle, and criadillas in Spain, Argentina and much of Mexico [1]. Similar dishes use lamb, pig or turkey testicles [1].

The dish is described as purported cowboy fare tied to ranching families; the culinary use is a by-product of livestock castration [1]. Several US towns hold testicle festivals, including Eagle, Idaho, and Virginia City, Nevada [1]. Many people regard it as an aphrodisiac [1].

A 2019 study of beef variety meats measured vitamin K forms called menaquinones (MK4 to MK13) in raw and cooked organ meats, because animal-derived menaquinones had been poorly characterised [2]. This concerns vitamin K content, not testosterone.

card.summary: Fried bull testicles eaten as a virility food; popular as lore, with no human data on testosterone.
card.aka: Rocky Mountain oysters, prairie oysters, calf fries
card.note: No studies show a hormonal effect from eating testicles.

quick.overview:
Rocky Mountain oysters are fried bull testicles. Some people eat them as an organ meat they believe supports testosterone or virility.

The dish is mainly a regional food tradition, and many regard it as an aphrodisiac. No studies were found testing a hormonal effect.
quick.mechanism: The usual belief is that eating the organ transfers hormonal benefit (a "like supports like" idea). No published research was found supporting this.
quick.risks: No specific risks are described in the sources reviewed. As with any food, safety depends on preparation.
